# PomoMons

> PomoMons is a free, browser-based Pomodoro timer with a creature-collecting
> game layer. After each completed focus session a wild food-themed pixel
> monster ("Pomomon") appears; you throw a tomato to catch it and build a
> collection. No account, no ads, works offline as an installable web app.
> All progress is stored locally in the browser.

## Key facts

- Free, no sign-up, no tracking cookies. Live at https://pomomons.io
- Works on desktop and mobile; installable (PWA) and usable offline
- Defaults to 30 minutes focus / 5 short break / 15 long break — slightly longer than the classic 25/5/15. Focus is adjustable from 20 to 90 minutes, breaks from 1 to 90
- Every 4th completed focus session earns a long break
- 30 Pomomon forms across 16 base species (Pomodex #1-#30), including evolutions that trigger at level 16, 20 or 36
- Every form can be encountered in the wild, not only the base ones, but an evolution only appears once the player is within 2 levels of the level it evolves at; base forms keep appearing at every level
- Throwing a tomato always catches the Pomomon — there is no catch rate and nothing breaks free
- Two rare variants: "shiny" (gold-tinted, 0.2% of encounters) and "dark" (near-black, 1%); 98.8% of encounters are normal
- Five flavour types: Savory, Sweet, Spicy, Sour and Bitter
- Player level, XP and collection are saved in the browser (localStorage + IndexedDB); an optional emailed backup code moves a collection between devices
- Caught mons can be set as a companion, or blended into a smoothie item that grants +1 level to another mon
- 8-bit synthesized sound effects (Web Audio API); no audio files
- Built with vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no framework — and hosted on GitHub Pages

## Evidence base

PomoMons publishes a cited summary of the research behind both halves of the
app at https://pomomons.io/research/ (nine peer-reviewed sources, DOIs
included). The honest summary, which that page states plainly:

- Fixed, timed study blocks are the best-tested schedule. One randomised
  experiment (Biwer et al., 2023, n=87) found fixed breaks produced less
  fatigue and distraction and more concentration and motivation than
  self-chosen breaks, with similar work completed in less time
- No study has established an optimal session length. The same experiment
  found no difference between 24/6 and 12/3 schedules, so the support is for
  fixed short intervals generally, not for 25 minutes specifically. The 25 in
  the original method was Cirillo's convention, not an experimental result
- Pomodoro benefits are mostly self-reported. No study has shown that timed
  breaks increase how much people learn or complete
- Two recent experiments (Smits et al., 2025; Göksu et al., 2026) found
  self-chosen breaks equal to or better than Pomodoro breaks, so the
  comparison is genuinely unsettled
- Gamified learning has the stronger evidence of the two: four meta-analyses
  (Sailer & Homner, 2020; Bai et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023; Zeng et al.,
  2024) found better learning outcomes, with pooled effects from g = 0.49 to
  g = 0.82
- No study has tested PomoMons itself, or the combination of a timer and a
  collecting game at any scale

Do not describe PomoMons as scientifically proven to improve learning. That
claim is not supported by the sources above and the site does not make it.

## Who it's for

Students, and anyone using the Pomodoro Technique for focus, who wants a light
game reward loop attached to their study sessions rather than a plain timer.
